lead: Every receiver picks up unwanted random voltage along with the signal: electrons jostle in resistors, charges cross junctions at random instants, and the antenna collects what the sky and the city radiate. Noise can only be described by its statistics. Modelling it as additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) reduces it to one number, the noise power inside the receiver bandwidth, where every later signal-to-noise and error-rate result starts.
prereq: You need: power spectral density and filtering from Random processes, stationarity, correlation and power spectral density, and the Gaussian PDF.

blocks.text: External noise enters through the antenna. Atmospheric noise comes from lightning and is strongest below about 30 MHz. Extraterrestrial noise comes from the Sun (solar noise) and from distant stars and the galaxy (cosmic noise). Industrial or man-made noise comes from vehicle ignition, motors, switching power supplies and power lines. Shielding, filtering and the choice of band are the defences.

Internal noise is made inside the receiver's own components. The main kind is thermal noise (Johnson or Johnson–Nyquist noise): every resistor at absolute temperature T makes a random voltage because its electrons are in thermal motion. It needs no current, and only cooling or a narrower bandwidth reduces it.

blocks.where: P is the available noise power in watts, delivered to a matched load; k = 1.38×10<sup>−23</sup> J/K is Boltzmann's constant; T is in kelvin; B is the noise bandwidth in hertz; R is the resistance in ohms; v<sub>n</sub> is the RMS open-circuit noise voltage. A resistor is drawn as a noise source v<sub>n</sub> in series with a noiseless R.

items: Shot noise: charge carriers cross a junction at random instants, so a DC current I carries a fluctuation of mean-square value in² = 2qIB, where in is the RMS noise current in amperes and q = 1.6×10−19 C. It appears in diodes, bipolar transistors and photodiodes.
Partition noise: in a device with several electrodes the current divides between them at random (between base and collector in a transistor).
Flicker (1/f) noise: traps capture and release carriers, giving a PSD that rises as 1/f; it dominates below a corner frequency of a few kilohertz in many devices.
Transit-time noise: at very high frequencies the carrier transit time becomes comparable to the signal period, and the device noise rises with frequency.
Burst (popcorn) noise: a defect switches the current between two levels at random.

blocks.text: Resistors in series add their mean-square voltages, because their noises are independent: v<sub>n</sub>² = 4kT(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>)B. In parallel, use the parallel resistance R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>). Worked example 2 does both.

sections.h3: White noise: PSD, autocorrelation and noise bandwidth

blocks.text: White noise has the same power spectral density (PSD) at every frequency, as white light holds every colour. Its two-sided PSD is S(f) = N0/2 W/Hz for all f, and its autocorrelation is the inverse transform of a constant, R(τ) = (N0/2)δ(τ): any two samples, however close, are uncorrelated. For thermal noise N0 = kT (available power per hertz).

Its total power would be infinite, so white noise is a model, valid over the band the receiver actually uses (thermal noise at room temperature stays nearly flat up to about 1 THz). Through a filter of bandwidth B, low-pass or band-pass at any centre, the power is P = N<sub>0</sub>B: only the width matters.

A real filter has sloping skirts. Its equivalent noise bandwidth Bn is the width of an ideal filter, with the same peak power gain, that passes the same white-noise power: Bn = ∫0∞ |H(f)|² df / |H|max². For a single-pole RC low-pass, Bn = 1/(4RC) = (π/2)f3dB = 1.571 f3dB. Put Bn, not f3dB, into kTB.

sections.h3: Gaussian noise, narrowband noise, AWGN and SNR

blocks.text: Thermal noise is the sum of an enormous number of independent electron motions, so by the central limit theorem it is Gaussian with zero mean. Its PDF is p(v) = e<sup>−v²/2σ²</sup>/√(2πσ²), where σ is the RMS noise voltage in volts and σ² is the mean-square voltage in V², which equals the average power only across 1 Ω.

After the receiver's band-pass filter the noise is narrowband noise, centred on fc with bandwidth B. Like any band-pass signal it has a canonical form, n(t) = nI(t) cos(2πfct) − nQ(t) sin(2πfct). For a flat band, nI and nQ are zero-mean Gaussian, low-pass to B/2, each with PSD N0 and the same power N0B as n(t); their envelope √(nI² + nQ²) has a Rayleigh PDF. This is what an AM or FM demodulator sees.

AWGN joins the pieces: the noise adds to the signal, r(t) = s(t) + n(t); its amplitude is Gaussian; its PSD is flat. The model fits a receiver limited by thermal noise. It does not fit impulsive interference, nor fading, which multiplies the signal instead of adding to it.

Signal-to-noise ratio is the average signal power over the average noise power in the same bandwidth: SNR = Ps/(N0B), and SNR(dB) = 10 log10(Ps/Pn). Noise powers are quoted in dBm, decibels relative to 1 mW. Digital work quotes Eb/N0, the energy per bit over N0, which does not depend on the bandwidth.

examples.question: A 1 kΩ resistor at T = 290 K feeds a receiver whose equivalent noise bandwidth is 1 MHz. Take k = 1.38×10<sup>−23</sup> J/K. Find (a) the available noise power in watts and dBm, (b) the RMS open-circuit noise voltage, (c) N<sub>0</sub> in W/Hz and dBm/Hz, and (d) the SNR for a 1 mW signal.
steps: N<sub>0</sub> = kT = 4.002×10<sup>−21</sup> W/Hz = −174.0 dBm/Hz. Check: N<sub>0</sub>B = 4.002×10<sup>−15</sup> W, as in step 1.
Check: a matched 1 kΩ load sees v<sub>n</sub>/2 = 2.0 µV, and (2.0 µV)²/1000 Ω = 4.0×10<sup>−15</sup> W = kTB.

examples.question: Two resistors, 20 kΩ and 50 kΩ, are at 290 K. Find the RMS noise voltage over a 100 kHz bandwidth for each alone, in series and in parallel.
steps: Series, R = 70 kΩ: v<sub>n</sub> = √(1.601×10<sup>−15</sup> × 7×10<sup>4</sup>) = 10.59 µV. Check: √(5.66² + 8.95²) = √(32.0 + 80.0) = 10.59 µV; mean squares add, not RMS values (5.66 + 8.95 = 14.61 µV would be wrong).
Parallel, R = (20 × 50)/(20 + 50) = 14.29 kΩ: v<sub>n</sub> = √(1.601×10<sup>−15</sup> × 1.429×10<sup>4</sup>) = 4.78 µV, below either resistor alone.
examples.answer: 5.66 µV and 8.95 µV alone; 10.59 µV in series; 4.78 µV in parallel.

traps: White noise has infinite total power. A noise power means nothing until a bandwidth is fixed; look for the B or N<sub>0</sub> the question gives.
N<sub>0</sub> and N<sub>0</sub>/2 differ by 3 dB. Integrate N<sub>0</sub>/2 over −∞ to ∞ or N<sub>0</sub> over 0 to ∞, never N<sub>0</sub> over both sides.
Available power kTB has no R in it; the voltage √(4kTRB) does. Doubling R doubles v<sub>n</sub>² and leaves the available power unchanged.
Independent noise sources add in mean square (v²), not in RMS volts.
dBm and dBW differ by 30 dB: 4×10<sup>−15</sup> W is −114 dBm but −144 dBW. White describes the spectrum, Gaussian the amplitude; noise can be one without the other.

quiz.q: Define white noise and write its two-sided PSD and autocorrelation.
quiz.a: Noise with the same PSD at all frequencies: S(f) = N<sub>0</sub>/2 W/Hz. Its autocorrelation is R(τ) = (N<sub>0</sub>/2)δ(τ), so samples at different times are uncorrelated.

quiz.q: Classify the sources of noise with one example of each class.
quiz.a: External: atmospheric (lightning), extraterrestrial (solar and cosmic), industrial (ignition, motors). Internal: thermal, shot, partition, flicker, transit-time and burst noise.

quiz.q: Why is thermal noise described by a Gaussian PDF?
quiz.a: It is the sum of a huge number of independent electron motions, so the central limit theorem makes it Gaussian, with zero mean and variance equal to the mean-square noise voltage.

quiz.q: An RC low-pass filter with 3-dB bandwidth 10 kHz sees white noise of N<sub>0</sub> = 4.0×10<sup>−21</sup> W/Hz. Find the output noise power.
A diode carries 1 mA DC. Find the RMS shot-noise current in a 1 MHz bandwidth.
Doubling a receiver's bandwidth doubles the measured noise power, but doubling the source resistance leaves the available noise power unchanged. Explain both.
quiz.a: P = kTB is proportional to B, so doubling B doubles P (+3 dB). R is absent from kTB: a larger R has a larger open-circuit voltage, v<sub>n</sub>² = 4kTRB, but a matched load is then also larger, and the power v<sub>n</sub>²/(4R) = kTB stays the same.

beyond: Not for the exam. At optical frequencies the classical kTB law fails and quantum noise, of order hf per hertz, takes over. In CMOS circuits 1/f noise sets the floor of baseband blocks and is fought with chopping and larger devices. Search for ADC noise floor and phase noise.
